title: Build it for real
desc: Your own routine: drafted, dry-run, activated, and watched on its first run.
learningGoal: After this lesson you have one routine of your own that is active and has completed a live run — and you can read the dry-run panel, the activation refusal and the run log well enough to fix the next one yourself.

steps.title: Pick something small enough to finish today
steps.bodyMd:
Most first routines are never switched on: the one people pick is too big to finish, so it stays a draft nobody trusts.

Nadia runs operations at **Van Dijk Groep**, a 60-person Dutch installation firm. Three jobs annoy her every week; she is building **one** of them today.

A first routine you can finish has three properties:

- **One trigger** — every routine has exactly one primary trigger, so the job needs one clear starting moment.
- **Data you already have** — a table, an inbox, a form you control.
- **One destination** — one notification, one row, one document. Not "and it also updates four systems".

Her pick: *every Monday at 08:00, read the open quotes from the `offertes` table, have AI write five bullets, notify the sales lead.* A trigger and three steps. Nothing irreversible.

steps.question: Nadia has three candidates. Which one is the right first build — the one she can get live today?

choices.label: Monday 08:00: read the open rows from the quotes table, have AI summarise them, send the sales lead a notification.
Every invoice mail with a PDF: scan it for personal data, extract six fields, ask the purchasing manager to approve anything over 2500 euro, then write a table row.
choices.feedback: A fine routine — for next month. It needs an app-event trigger with a working filter, an extraction step, a branch and a second person to press Approve before you ever see it finish. Too many things that can be wrong at once for a first build.

choices.label: "Make the Monday admin less annoying."
choices.feedback: That is a complaint, not a job. A routine needs a starting moment, an input and a destination. Without those three there is nothing to put on the canvas.

choices.label: Replace the whole quoting process end to end, so nobody has to touch it again.
choices.feedback: A routine that replaces a process has to be right the first time or people lose trust in it. Start with something whose worst failure is a missing notification.

steps.explanation: One trigger, data that already exists, one destination. Option A is four steps over a table she already keeps — small enough to dry-run, activate and check inside one morning.

steps.title: Two ways in — and they end in the same place
steps.bodyMd:
**By hand.** Open **Studio → Automations**, start a new routine, and the canvas asks *"What does this routine start with?"* — the seven trigger cards. Pick **Schedule**, then add steps from the ribbon. Every change autosaves: *"Changes save automatically."*

**With the assistant.** Start a new routine the same way, then press **Assistant** on the empty canvas, where it says *"Or describe the routine:"*. A chat opens beside the canvas. Describe the trigger and what should happen; the canvas narrates itself while it works (*"Building · 0:07 · Placing Gmail…"*) and editing is paused until it finishes.

Both roads end at the same door. **A routine the assistant just finished is still a draft.** Nothing fires until a person presses **Activate** — the builder tooling cannot switch a routine on, by design.

steps.title: Build it — we'll verify it
steps.instruction: Open Automations and build your routine: pick a trigger, add the steps, fill the fields. Every change autosaves, so there is nothing to press to keep it. Then press Dry-run (the left half of the Run split-button) and let it finish. Come back here when it has — this step checks again.

steps.title: Reading the dry-run panel
steps.bodyMd:
A dry-run is a full pass over your graph with **no real actions**. When it finishes, a drawer opens headed **Dry-run preview (success)** — or with whatever status it reached — and every node on the canvas now carries the input it received and the output it produced. Click a node and read both.

When a field is wrong, the node panel says so in two strengths:

- **"Fix this before the routine can run:"** — blocking. Activation will refuse.
- **"Worth checking:"** — a warning. It will run; it may not do what you meant.

Nadia's first dry-run stopped at the AI step: the summary prompt still pointed at the table step's whole output instead of its rows.

steps.title: Five things the panel is telling you
steps.instruction: Your own dry-run is open. Match each signal on the canvas to what it actually means for you right now.

pairs.left: A step listed under "Fix this before the routine can run:"
pairs.right: Clear it now — Activate will refuse
pairs.note: The blocking list is the one that decides whether you get to switch the routine on at all. Work through it before you read anything else.

pairs.right: It will run — it may not do what you meant
pairs.note: A warning never stops activation. It is the polite way of saying nobody can tell from the definition whether this is right; only you know.

pairs.left: Your notification step reports success in the dry-run panel
pairs.note: Side-effecting actions are synthesised rather than executed, so their green tick is about the call being well-formed, not about delivery.

pairs.left: A Code step's output lists what it "would have called"
pairs.right: The code ran, its outside calls did not
pairs.note: In a dry-run the code itself runs, so a typo or a crash shows up now. Every call it makes to the outside is only recorded and answered with a placeholder, so whatever it did with that answer is not real data yet.

pairs.left: A Privacy Shield step carries a "would block" annotation
pairs.right: Harmless here, a stopped run live
pairs.note: In a dry-run a Shield block is downgraded to an annotation instead of failing the run. Read it now, or find out on Monday.

steps.title: Turn the green tick into a Monday checklist
steps.bodyMd:
The dry-run proved the **shape** — the steps connect, the bindings resolve, the fields are there. Everything it could not touch becomes one line on a checklist for the first live run.

Walk your own canvas once and write down, per step, what you will look at afterwards:

- **Every action step** — was it synthesised? Then check the destination itself: the inbox, the channel, the table row.
- **A Call a web service step with a saved credential** — the call is synthesised, so the credential is never decrypted and never proved. An expired one passes a dry-run and fails live.
- **A Code step**: its code ran, but every outside call it makes was only recorded. Its first real call is Monday's.
- **Every "would block" annotation** — decide now whether that data should be there at all.

Nadia's list came to three lines. That is the list she will read the run log against.

steps.title: Your turn: the handover note for your routine
steps.instruction: Write the note you would leave a colleague who has to keep your routine running, in three parts. One: what it does — the trigger, the steps in order, and where the result lands. Two: what the dry-run showed — the status, anything listed under "Fix this before the routine can run:" or "Worth checking:", and what you changed. Three: your Monday checklist — for each step the dry-run could not really execute, the one place you will look to confirm it worked, named exactly (which screen, which filter, what you expect to see).
steps.placeholder: e.g. Weekly on Monday 08:00 it reads open rows from the offertes table, has an AI step write five bullets and notifies the sales lead. The dry-run first said "Fix this before the routine can run:" on the AI step — the prompt bound the whole table output instead of the rows field; I re-bound it and it went green. Monday checklist: (1) Runs & log, mode Live runs, expect one row Outcome Succeeded, Started by On a schedule; (2) the sales lead's notification actually arrived — I will ask her.

steps.question: Nadia presses Activate and the server refuses. Which of these is something the strict activation pass really objects to?

choices.label: A step with a required field still empty.
The routine has no description.
choices.feedback: Description is optional — it is only "Shown to admins reviewing this automation." Nothing about activation requires it.

choices.label: The last dry-run was more than a day ago.
choices.feedback: Activation never looks at when you last dry-ran. It re-validates the definition itself: tools, required inputs, knowledge-base links and the schedule.

choices.label: A step whose output no later step uses.
choices.feedback: An unused output is untidy, not invalid. The pass reads the definition itself: unknown or unpermitted tools, empty required inputs, an unauthorised knowledge base, and a schedule with no upcoming run time.

steps.explanation: Saving a draft only checks that the routine holds together; **Activate** is the strict pass. It refuses an unknown or unpermitted tool, an empty required input, a knowledge base you may not use, or a schedule with no upcoming run time. One thing it lets through with a warning: a step **pinned** to saved sample data. That routine goes live serving the sample instead of running the step — so read the warning rather than clicking past it.

steps.title: The first live run, watched
steps.bodyMd:
**Studio → Runs & log** — *"Every time a routine fired: what started it, what it did, and what went wrong."*

Two things surprise people here:

- The **mode** filter defaults to **Live runs**, so the dry-runs you just did are hidden. Switch it to **Tests only** or **Live runs and tests** to see them.
- The **Now running** strip covers a fixed **last 24 hours**, whatever range chip the table is on.

The table has six labelled columns — **Outcome**, **What ran**, **What happened**, **Started**, **Took**, **Started by** — plus a hover menu on the rows you own. *Started by* reads **On a schedule** for a scheduled run and **Test run** for a dry-run. Open a run and the **Steps** rail replays it step by step, against the version of the routine that ran, not today's.

steps.title: Monday 08:04 — it failed
steps.instruction: Put the moves in the order a builder actually makes them.

items.label: Open Runs & log and click the Failures chip
Open the run and find the red row in the Steps rail, with its input and error
Use "Open in editor" and fix that step
Go back to the failed run and press "Run it again"

sim.feedback: Diagnose before you touch anything. The run tells you which step stopped it and on what data — the rail even marks it: "This is where it stopped. Nothing ran after this point." Fix, prove it with a dry-run, then retry; "Run it again" uses the routine as it is now, so it picks up your fix.

steps.question: That failing step is a flaky web service — it works nine mornings out of ten. With nothing configured, what happens on the tenth?

choices.label: The run stops at that step and is recorded as Failed — nothing retries by itself, so you read the error and press Run it again yourself.
Bee Flow retries the step a few times with a backoff before giving up.
choices.feedback: Retry is opt-in per step, and nothing is configured here: with no retry set, the first failure is the last attempt. Where a step does retry, every attempt is recorded, so a flaky tool stays visible in the log instead of hiding behind a green run.

choices.label: The step is skipped and the rest of the routine carries on.
choices.feedback: Nothing downstream runs. The Steps rail says it plainly: "This is where it stopped. Nothing ran after this point."

choices.label: The schedule notices the failure and fires the routine again shortly after.
choices.feedback: A schedule only fires at its next slot — next Monday, in this case. It has no idea the last run failed.

steps.explanation: Plan for failure explicitly. Two ways: set a retry on that step, or wire its failure output down a fallback path — ask the assistant for one and its activity log reads *"Added a fallback for failures"*. A run that absorbs a failure that way still finishes, and the log marks it **Recovered** with the number of problems handled. With neither, the error notification (on by default) tells you, and you press **Run it again**.

steps.title: Switch it on and let it run once
steps.instruction: Press Activate in the builder header. If your routine is on a schedule and you do not want to wait for its slot, open the Run menu next to Dry-run and choose Run live. Then open Runs & log and confirm one live run finished.

steps.title: Findable again in three months
steps.bodyMd:
The routine works. Now make it workable for the version of you who has forgotten all this.

- **Name it like a sentence** — "Monday pipeline briefing to sales" beats "Weekly digest v2". The name is what the run log shows under *What ran*.
- **Use a folder.** Folders are organisation-wide labels; removing one leaves the routines alone (*"Remove this folder — the automations in it stay"*) and returns them to the top level.
- **Check Settings → Notifications.** *On error* is on by default, *On success* is off. Turn success on for the first few weeks if you want the receipt.
- **Saved versions** keeps earlier designs with *View diff* and *Restore this version* — so edit without fear.
- Run history is kept **90 days**: the log answers "did it run in August?", not forever.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
You have a routine that exists, is switched on, and has run.

- **Build and prove.** Draft on the canvas or with the assistant, dry-run it, clear everything under *"Fix this before the routine can run:"*, and leave the panel with a written checklist of what only a live run can confirm.
- **Ship deliberately.** Activation is a human decision — nothing the assistant builds fires by itself — and it re-validates the whole definition before it lets anything go live.
- **Watch and repair.** Runs & log tells you what started it, what happened and where it stopped — then *Open in editor*, dry-run, *Run it again*.

Next chapter: writing the brief that makes all of this go faster.

ex-automation-hands-on-dryrun.title: Handover note and Monday checklist
ex-automation-hands-on-dryrun.task: The learner built a routine and dry-ran it, then wrote a handover note: what it does (trigger, steps, destination), what the dry-run showed (status, anything blocking or worth checking, what they changed), and a checklist for the first live run naming, per untested step, the exact place they will look to confirm it worked.
criteria: Names a concrete trigger and a concrete destination for a specific routine — not a goal or a wish.
Reports a real dry-run outcome: the status, and either something that was flagged and how it was fixed, or an honest 'nothing was flagged'.
The checklist is tied to steps of THIS routine that a dry-run could not really execute — a synthesised action, a code step's recorded outside calls, a credentialled call, a 'would block' annotation.
Each checklist line names where they will look and what they expect to see — a screen, a filter or chip, an outcome, or the destination itself — specific enough for a colleague to follow.
ex-automation-hands-on-dryrun.guidance: Pass work that is clearly about the learner's own routine, with named steps or fields, and whose part three someone else could actually carry out. Do not pass a generic essay about dry-running with no routine in it; do not pass an answer missing the trigger or the destination; do not pass a checklist of intentions ('check it worked', 'see if the mail arrived') with no screen, filter or destination named. Treating a synthesised green tick as proof the mail was sent fails criterion three. A dry-run that genuinely passed clean is fine, as long as the checklist is specific.

practiceTopic.title: Shipping a routine: dry-run, activate, watch
practiceTopic.summary: How a routine goes from draft to live in Bee Flow, and how to read the dry-run panel, the activation refusal and the run log.
facts: A dry-run executes the graph with no real actions: side-effecting actions are synthesised, code steps run with their outside calls only recorded, and a Privacy Shield block becomes a 'would block' annotation instead of a failure.
A routine the AI builder finished is still a draft and inactive; only a person pressing Activate makes it live.

Activation runs a strict pass and refuses on unknown or unpermitted tools, empty required inputs, an unauthorised knowledge base, and a schedule with no upcoming run time; a step pinned to saved sample data is only warned about, and then serves that sample on every live run.
The node panel separates blocking problems under 'Fix this before the routine can run:' from warnings under 'Worth checking:'.
In Studio → Runs & log the mode filter defaults to 'Live runs', so dry-runs are hidden until you switch to 'Tests only' or 'Live runs and tests'.
There is no automatic retry — retry is opt-in per step; otherwise a failed step stops the run and the Steps rail marks it 'This is where it stopped. Nothing ran after this point.'
Run notifications default to On error on and On success off, and run history is kept for 90 days.
Folders are organisation-wide labels; removing a folder leaves its routines in place and returns them to the top level.

actionChecks.label: Activate a routine and complete one live run
actionChecks.hint: In Studio → Automations, press Activate in the builder header, then run it live (or wait for its trigger) and confirm the run in Runs & log.

endpoints.returns: { automations: [...] } — the caller's own routines, each with id, title, isActive, isDraft, triggerType, lastStatus

criteria.label: A routine of yours is switched on
criteria.hint: Open the routine and press Activate in the builder header — the toggle then reads Pause.
criteria.rule: GET /api/automation/ has at least one row with isActive === true and isDraft === false
